rv.q: That emotion figures palpably in 'Fatherland,' a finely calibrated, surprisingly affecting new work of verbatim theater at New York City Center Stage II.
Fatherland is as taut as a tightrope and superbly acted.
Battitta gives the most memorable performance of all, delivering a one-man reenactment of the January 6 riots that radiates pure adrenaline.
But the result was that I’m no further along in understanding what’s been happening in this country.
All in all, the show’s dependence on reenacted situations, with their sometimes excessive emoting, more than on courtroom process, creates something of a dramatic imbalance.
Fatherland is a solid courtroom recreation without much in the way of high moments of drama.
The play, conceived and directed by Fountain Theatre artistic director Stephen Sachs, chooses to focus on Jackson Reffitt, the perpetrator’s 19-year-old son.
What makes Fatherland so remarkable is the verbatim text still allowing for subtext and role reversals and characters who grow and change.
With breakneck pacing and powerful performances from its two leads, the production rips the bandage off a wounded moment in our history.
Sachs nonetheless crafts a gripping, and troubling, family drama.
“Fatherland” succeeds in showing how some of the puzzle pieces fit into the larger scheme of chaos.

cn.t: This verbatim docudrama about a Jan. 6 rioter turned in by his own son earns praise for its timely, unsettling examination of American division, though some critics find the documentary format unconvincing.

vr.q: Fatherland manages to be incredibly tense and gripping in a way that I didn't expect it to be.
